headline: Dog Days on the River — Bass Go Deep, Snappers Take Over the Coves
subhead: With the shad long gone upriver and the water pushing into the mid-70s, the lower Connecticut settles into its slow, warm-water summer rhythm.
body_markdown:
The greenheads are thick in the marsh grass off Old Lyme this week, which tells you everything you need to know about where we are in the season. Shad are a memory now — those big roe fish that packed the river back in April, working up past Essex toward the Enfield rapids, they're long gone, scattered somewhere between here and the headwaters of Massachusetts and Vermont, doing what shad do this time of year, which is nothing anyone on this river gets to see. That run feels like a lifetime ago by the time you're standing on the rocks at Saybrook Point in July with sweat running into your eyes and the marsh smelling like low tide and cut grass.

This is the slow season on the lower river, and I mean that in the way an old-timer means it — not dead, just patient. The river's running low and warm, the current soft on the ebb, and with Long Island Sound holding in the low 70s off Kings Point and high 60s off New London, our water at the mouth here isn't far behind. I'd put the flow off Saybrook Point in the mid-70s most afternoons, and that number matters, because striped bass don't love water that warm. They tolerate it. Above 72 or so they start looking for relief — deeper water, moving current, shade under a dock, anything that isn't direct sun on shallow flats.

What that means on the water is simple: the good bass fishing has shrunk down to a window. Dawn, dusk, and full dark. I've had better luck the last two weeks working the channel edge off the Baldwin Bridge and the deep bend below Essex right at first light, before the sun gets up over the trees and starts cooking the flats. Live eels drifted on the current seams, or bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig tight to the bottom where the channel drops off — that's been the program. Nothing explosive, but a couple of solid fish in the 28 to 34-inch range have come off that stretch on the outgoing tide, right as the current starts really moving water out past Great Island.

Speaking of Great Island — that's still the nursery it's always been, and right now it's snapper blue water, plain and simple. Those young bluefish are thick in the coves and guts behind the island, chasing whatever's small and silver in three and four feet of water. If you've got a kid who wants steady action, small silver spoons or a piece of squid on a bare hook under a bobber back in those channels will keep a rod bent all afternoon. It's not glamorous fishing but it's honest fishing, and it's about the best bet going in the heat of the day when the bigger stuff has gone quiet.

White perch are doing what they always do in late summer — working the marsh creeks and the slower water up around the DEP Marina in Old Lyme, taking small jigs and worms fished slow along the bottom. Nothing trophy-sized, but a mixed bag of perch and the occasional small bass in that same stretch has been enough to make an evening worthwhile, especially with the bugs backing off once the sun drops.

The bigger bluefish — the choppers — have shown up sporadically at the outer bar off the river mouth when there's bait around, usually bunker pushed in tight by the tide. I heard of a run of them working the rip off Saybrook Point for about twenty minutes on an outgoing tide last week, enough to turn a slow morning into a good one for whoever happened to be positioned right with a metal jig in hand. That's the nature of it this time of year — short, sharp windows, not sustained action. You need to be in position when the tide and the bait line up, and then you need a little luck.

We flagged this pattern last week — said conditions would hold stable and that the warm-water bass pattern would persist as long as the weather stayed put — and that's exactly the week we got. No fronts, no big wind shift, just steady heat and a river settling into its summer groove. I don't expect much to change over the next several days either. The moon's building back toward the new moon on August 12th, which means tides will start pushing a little harder as we get into next week, and that extra current could help stir things up at the mouth and around Great Island. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be at the Baldwin Bridge current seam an hour before first light with an eel in my hand, working the last of the dark before the sun starts pushing that water temperature back up. After that, I'd be looking for shade, a cold drink, and waiting for the tide to turn again after dark.
